strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap between weak PIT-based calibration and restrictive parametric recalibration approaches (e.g., Song et al. 2019 GPBETA), with clear articulation of why marginal PIT calibration is insufficient (error cancellation argument).

Solid theoretical foundation: the calibration-sharpness decomposition (Lemma 4.1) via generalized conditional mutual information, and the auto-calibration/sharpness-preservation guarantee for the population-level recalibration map (Proposition 5.2), are both proven rigorously in the appendix and connect cleanly to existing notions (grouping loss of Kull & Flach, proper scoring rule theory of Gneiting & Raftery).

The proposed Energy Distance Kernel reduces the cost of evaluating distributional kernels from O(n^2) to O(n log n) for real-valued targets, a practically useful and non-trivial contribution for scaling nonparametric distribution-valued regression.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many UCI datasets, four base model classes (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF), and multiple recalibration baselines (PIT, GPBETA), with rigorous statistical testing (SKCE auto-calibration test, KS-based PIT test) rather than relying only on point-estimate calibration metrics.

Thoughtful set of supplementary analyses (comparison to conformal prediction, ablation on EDK efficiency, wall-clock comparisons, comparison to plain kernelized regression) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and demonstrate practical relevance.

Honest limitations section acknowledging the O(n_cal^3) scaling bottleneck, loss of explicit density representation, and the fact that auto-calibration is still weaker than full feature-conditional calibration.
weaknesses: The auto-calibration hypothesis test (Figure 1) has very different statistical power across datasets (explicitly noted by the authors via test-set sizes in parentheses), so acceptance/rejection rates are not directly comparable across datasets, making the headline claim that CKME 'consistently outperforms' somewhat qualitative; no correction or power-adjusted analysis is provided across the many dataset x model x method combinations.

The empirical CRPS results (Table 1, Fig. 2) show CKME sometimes substantially *worsens* predictive score relative to the uncalibrated baseline (e.g., yacht: 1.276–1.614x, housing: up to 1.19x across base models), which is in tension with the paper's theoretical claim (Proposition 5.2) that recalibration preserves sharpness; this population-level guarantee clearly does not translate cleanly to the finite-sample estimator, and this gap is not analyzed (e.g., no variance/bias study of the CKME estimator or the simplex-projection pre-image heuristic).

The distributional pre-image step is solved via a simplification (Euclidean projection to the simplex rather than the stated RKHS-weighted quadratic program in Eq. 39), justified only as an implementation convenience; the impact of this approximation on the calibration/sharpness guarantees is not empirically quantified.

Scalability remains a real concern: O(n_cal^3) complexity from kernel ridge regression is acknowledged but not mitigated (e.g., no low-rank/Nystrom approximation experiments), limiting applicability to larger calibration sets than tested here.

Kernel bandwidth (median heuristic) and only the regularization parameter are tuned; no sensitivity analysis is provided for how kernel choice/bandwidth affects calibration outcomes, which is important for a method whose entire behavior hinges on kernel design.

Remark 5.3 requires Y to be a compact metric space for the universal Gaussian-type kernel, which is not strictly satisfied by unbounded real-valued targets used throughout the experiments (e.g., UCI regression targets); this technical mismatch between assumptions and practice is not discussed.

PIT recalibration remains the strongest method for PIT-calibration (Fig. 3) and is much cheaper computationally; the paper could more directly quantify the practical trade-off (cost vs. calibration-strength gain) an end user faces when choosing CKME over the simpler, well-established PIT approach.

strengths: The paper provides a coherent theoretical framework linking proper scoring rules, calibration, and sharpness via a generalized conditional mutual information decomposition (Lemma 4.1), with rigorous proofs in the appendix.

The proposed Energy Distance Kernel (EDK) offering O(n log n) evaluation for real-valued targets is a genuinely useful practical contribution that addresses a real scalability bottleneck of kernel-based distribution regression.

The experimental protocol is comprehensive: multiple base models (GDN, MDN, BNN, DRF), many UCI datasets of varying size, comparisons against PIT and GPBETA baselines, plus supplementary comparisons to conformal prediction and standard kernelized regression in the appendix.

The paper correctly identifies and clearly articulates a genuine weakness of existing PIT-based calibration (marginal error cancellation) and situates the contribution well against closely related prior work (Song et al. 2019, Moskvichev & Sejdinovic 2025, Gruber & Buettner 2024).
weaknesses: The abstract's claim that the method 'consistently outperforms prior re-calibration approaches' is not well supported by Table 1: CKME frequently produces substantially worse CRPS than the uncalibrated baseline and other recalibration methods on several datasets (e.g., yacht, housing, concrete across multiple base models show CKME CRPS ratios >1.1-1.6), indicating a real sharpness cost that is understated in the framing of the results.

The improved SKCE test acceptance rates for CKME (Figure 1) could be confounded by reduced test power if CKME predictions are less sharp (wider/more diffuse); the paper does not rule out that its apparent calibration advantage is partly an artifact of lower statistical power rather than genuinely better auto-calibration, despite claiming that sharpness is preserved by Proposition 5.2 (which only holds asymptotically/in the population limit, not necessarily for the finite-sample simplex-projected estimator actually used).

The practical algorithm relies on a heuristic Euclidean projection onto the simplex (Appendix C, Eq. 40) rather than the theoretically justified weighted projection (Eq. 39), which is an approximation without accompanying error bounds or convergence analysis, weakening the link between the theoretical guarantees (auto-calibration, sharpness preservation) and what is actually deployed.

Remark 5.3 requires Y to be a compact metric space for the Gaussian-type kernel to be universal/characteristic, yet the main proposed EDK is applied to Y = R (an unbounded, non-compact space) in all experiments; this theoretical inconsistency is not addressed or reconciled.

The comparison to GPBETA may be unfair, since its official implementation forces a Gaussian approximation of the base model's output regardless of the base model's true predictive form, potentially handicapping it relative to CKME, which is not similarly constrained.

The method's output collapses to an empirical distribution supported only on calibration-set target values, discarding continuous density structure even when the base model provides one; this is a significant practical limitation for downstream applications needing density evaluation, and is only briefly acknowledged.

The core theoretical decomposition (Section 4) is explicitly stated to quantitatively coincide with the pre-existing grouping loss decomposition of Kull & Flach (2015), limiting the novelty of this contribution to a re-derivation/reframing rather than a new result.

Standard kernel methods here scale O(n_cal^3), a substantial limitation for larger calibration sets, and the paper does not explore mitigations (e.g., Nyström approximation, random features) despite this being a well-known scalability issue in the CKME literature.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: existing regression recalibration methods either use weak PIT-based calibration or restrictive parametric assumptions (Song et al. 2019); the paper proposes a fully nonparametric alternative grounded in auto-calibration, a provably stronger notion.

Solid theoretical contributions: a calibration-sharpness decomposition of expected score via a generalized conditional mutual information notion (Lemma 4.1), a proof that the CKME-based recalibration map achieves auto-calibration while preserving sharpness (Prop 5.2), and a formalization of the Gneiting et al. (2007) sharpness-subject-to-calibration conjecture (Prop B.1) — these connect cleanly to prior notions like grouping loss (Kull & Flach, 2015).

The proposed Energy Distance Kernel reduces the cost of comparing empirical predictive distributions from O(m^2) to O(m log m), a meaningful and practically useful efficiency contribution for real-valued targets.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 11 UCI-style datasets, 4 diverse base models (DRF, MDN, BNN, GDN), rigorous statistical hypothesis testing (SKCE, KS test) rather than only point calibration metrics, plus useful ablations (runtime vs. naive kernel, comparison to conformal prediction, comparison to plain kernel regression, wall-clock comparisons) in the appendix.

Honest and specific limitations section (O(n_cal^3) cost, loss of continuous density structure, targeting auto- rather than local/feature-conditional calibration), which strengthens rather than weakens the paper's credibility.
weaknesses: The recalibrated output is restricted to an empirical distribution supported on calibration-set targets (via projection of CKME weights onto the simplex), discarding any continuous density structure the base model had; the pre-image problem is solved only approximately (Euclidean projection rather than the stated RKHS-optimal quadratic program in Appendix C), and the effect of this approximation on sharpness/calibration is not directly quantified.

CRPS results (Table 1, Fig. 2) show the method sometimes producing large, non-trivial changes relative to the base model (e.g., large CRPS reductions on naval, but CRPS increases on wine for DRF/BNN with PIT/GPBETA and occasional degradation for CKME too), with substantial variance across splits, particularly for very small datasets (yacht, n=31) where hypothesis-test power is inherently low — this undercuts some of the strength of the headline claim of consistent improvement.

The GPBETA baseline is evaluated after approximating non-Gaussian base model outputs (MDN, DRF, BNN) with a single Gaussian fit to the first two moments, which likely disadvantages it in the comparison; while this stems from GPBETA's own restriction, it complicates a fully fair reading of the 'CKME outperforms GPBETA' claim.

Scalability is a real practical concern (O(n_cal^3) due to solving a linear system, plus O(n_cal^2) kernel evaluations), which the paper acknowledges but does not attempt to mitigate (e.g., via Nyström or random features), limiting applicability to large calibration sets.

The comparison against conformal prediction (Appendix D) relies on a single dependence measure (distance correlation between predicted intervals and PIT values) rather than a formal test, making the claimed advantage over CP more suggestive than rigorously established.

Presentation is dense and heavily appendix-reliant for core experimental protocol and results (e.g., detailed per-dataset benchmark figures, pre-image details, CP comparison), which may hinder accessibility for readers relying on the main text alone.
